analysis.one_liner: Requires 900-number services to disclose prices upfront, lets callers hang up free, and creates telephone billing dispute rights.
analysis.headline: Passed both chambers by voice vote with 14 Senate cosponsors split 8 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and became the Telephone Disclosure and Dispute Resolution Act of 1992.
analysis.plain_summary: Pay-per-call 900-number services — phone psychics, phone sex lines, sweepstakes hotlines, sports score lines — charged callers by the minute, billed them through their phone bills, and often left customers with surprise charges, threatened phone disconnection, or no recourse. This bill required the FCC and FTC to write rules forcing upfront price disclosures, a free hang-up window, refunds for illegal charges, the option to block 900 access, and a formal process to dispute telephone-billed charges. It passed with heavy bipartisan support and was enacted in 1992.
analysis.who_benefits: Households billed for 900-number calls: parents whose children called kid-targeted hotlines, people misled by sweepstakes and prize-promotion pitches, and customers who faced losing basic phone service over disputed pay-per-call charges. It also protects anyone whose phone bill carries third-party charges, since the billing dispute and credit-reporting rules apply to telephone-billed purchases generally.

how_it_helps.text: Every audiotext call must open with a disclosure describing the service, the total cost or per-minute rate, and other fees, and the caller can hang up at the end of that message without owing anything [S4].
Common carriers may not disconnect or interrupt a customer's local or long-distance phone service because of nonpayment for pay-per-call charges [S2,S5].

Local phone companies must offer subscribers the option to block all pay-per-call access, free of charge for a reasonable initial period, and the cost of blocking cannot be spread onto general ratepayers [S4].

Advertisers must clearly display the cost of calling, disclose the odds of winning any prize, state that minors need parental consent, and are barred from ads that emit tones that automatically dial a 900 number [S4,S5].

Customers can dispute telephone-billed charges in writing within 30 days; the carrier must investigate and correct or explain the bill within set deadlines, and a carrier that fails to comply forfeits the right to collect the disputed amount [S6].

Carriers cannot threaten a disputing customer's credit rating or report the amount as delinquent until they have met the dispute process and given the customer 20 days to pay, and must report any later resolution to anyone they initially reported to [S6].
Regulations must require refunds for callers billed for services that violated the rules or other consumer protection law [S4,S5].
State attorneys general can sue in federal court to stop violations and win damages for their residents [S4,S5].
The bill bans the manufacture or import of scanning receivers that can pick up cellular phone frequencies, protecting cellular callers from eavesdropping [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Pay-per-call providers bear compliance costs, mandatory disclosures, refunds, and the loss of revenue from practices aimed at children and from misleading prize promotions. Telephone carriers pay for disclosure mailings, toll-free help lines, blocking capability, and refunds, though they can recover compliance costs from providers. Scanner manufacturers lose the ability to sell cellular-capable scanners. Callers still pay for legitimate services they choose to use.

drawbacks.text: Telephone carriers receive broad protections: a carrier is exempt from civil or criminal liability merely for transmitting or billing for a violating pay-per-call service unless it knew the service broke the law, and carriers get a safe harbor from lawsuits for cutting off services in good-faith compliance [S5].
Blocking pay-per-call access is free only for an initial period set by the FCC; afterward the cost can be charged to the subscriber through contract or tariff [S4,S5].

The bill lets the FBI Director or a senior designee obtain a person's name, address, and toll billing records for foreign counterintelligence investigations based on a written certification rather than a court order, with only semiannual reports to Congress — a real privacy trade-off attached to a consumer bill [S5].
Title V exempts state-authorized lotteries from federal criminal restrictions on lottery advertising, expanding advertising for gambling products [S5].

The rules allow exemptions from the introductory disclosure message for frequent callers using a bypass mechanism and for services at nominal charges, weakening the disclosure guarantee for the heaviest users [S4].

The bill's stated findings explicitly aim to 'facilitate the growth of a robust and competitive pay-per-call marketplace,' so it protects consumers while also promoting the industry it regulates [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections address concrete, recurring harms — surprise per-minute charges, children racking up bills, misleading prize solicitations, and basic phone service held hostage over disputed 900 charges. The core disclosure, blocking, and dispute-resolution rights outweigh the compliance costs, which are modest and borne by the industry profiting from the calls. The weak points are the carrier liability shield and safe harbor, which leave customers with less recourse against the companies doing the billing, and the FBI records-access provision, which is unrelated to consumer protection and expands government access to phone records without a court order.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by voice vote — the Senate twice, and the House passed the Senate bill only after replacing its text with its own version — the Senate agreed to the House version with its own amendment, and the reconciled bill was enacted as the Telephone Disclosure and Dispute Resolution Act of 1992.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Inouye introduced the 900 Services Consumer Protection Act on July 29, 1991, and it was referred to the Commerce Committee [S8].
The Commerce Committee ordered it reported favorably with amendments the next day, and Sen. Hollings reported it to the Senate on October 16, 1991, with a written report [S8].
The Senate passed the bill with amendments by voice vote on October 29, 1991 [S8].

The House held the Senate bill at the desk from October 30, 1991, until February 25, 1992, when it struck out the Senate text and inserted its own similar measure, H.R. 3490, retitled the Telephone Disclosure and Dispute Resolution Act, and passed it without objection [S8,S4].
On October 7, 1992, the Senate concurred in the House amendment with a further substitute amendment by voice vote, and the message went to the House the next day [S8,S5].

The final version was enacted as the Telephone Disclosure and Dispute Resolution Act of 1992, carrying the pay-per-call consumer rules plus unrelated riders on cellular scanners, FBI records access, computer crime, and lottery advertising [S1,S5].

In the final Senate version, the consumer protections were preserved — carrier obligations, FTC advertising rules, and a billing dispute process modeled on credit-billing law — but carriers gained liability exemptions and cost-recovery rights that were not in the version as introduced [S2,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone customers and parents came out ahead: they got upfront price disclosure, free hang-ups, blocking options, protection from losing basic service over 900 disputes, and a formal billing dispute process. The pay-per-call industry also gained a federal framework and consumer confidence for its legitimate business, and carriers gained liability protections they did not have in the original Senate bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Phone customers; also legitimate pay-per-call operators

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded opposition: the Senate passed it twice by voice vote and the House passed it without objection, and its 14 Senate cosponsors split 8 Democrats and 6 Republicans [S7,S8].

industries.industry: Pay-per-call (audiotext) service providers — phone sex lines, psychics, prize and sweepstakes hotlines, sports and entertainment lines
industries.note: The bill bans the practices that generated much of the industry's revenue — hiding costs, billing callers who hang up, targeting children under 12, auto-dialing ad tones, misleading prize promotions — and forces refunds. At the same time, Congress wrote that the industry's legitimate growth depends on consumer confidence, so the law also legitimizes and stabilizes the pay-per-call marketplace [S6,S4].

industries.industry: Telephone common carriers (local and long-distance phone companies acting as billing and collection channels)
industries.note: The law locks in carriers as the permanent billing and collection channel for pay-per-call services, gives them a liability shield for carrying or billing violating services unless they knew, lets them recover compliance costs from providers, and shields them from suits for good-faith terminations — while requiring them to offer blocking, refunds, separate bill statements, and to keep basic service connected during 900-billing disputes [S5].

The bill bans manufacturing or importing scanners that can receive cellular phone frequencies or be readily altered to do so, ending that product line; the scanners' main use was listening to other people's cellular calls [S5].
The scanner ban protects cellular calls from interception, supporting subscriber privacy and confidence in cellular service [S5].

Title V exempts advertisements and information about lotteries authorized in a state from federal criminal restrictions on lottery advertising, expanding how these gambling products can be promoted [S5].
